O5.answer:
My lord — practical, then.

A single table, everyone at it, sightlines to every face. Actors reading to each other, not into paper, is most of the value; the moment someone is behind a pillar you have lost their scene.

One reader for stage directions, cast in advance, who does not act them. Hard copies, numbered scenes, same draft for every hand — a mixed-draft room wastes twenty minutes discovering it.

A clock running from the first line, and someone recording page-by-page timings, not just the total. The total tells you nothing you can act on. Second volume on pacing has the whole argument, but briefly: you want to know *where* the sag is.

A scribe who is not you and not the director, writing only what was heard, not what should be fixed.

No notes during. None. Read the thing end to end at performance pace — not skim pace, which flatters every scene — then break, then discuss.

Water on the table, a room booked forty minutes longer than the read, and phones collected or face-down. Decent acoustics matter more than comfort; a soft room makes weak delivery sound intentional.

And no one in the room who cannot resist speaking. That includes producers.

My lord, I hold with the watch — and I want to be clear that I am holding, not merely disagreeing before folding, because you have given me a preference rather than an argument. If there is an argument behind the lean I have not heard it yet, and I would like to.

The case, briefly. The close-up opens with a question in the frame: whose hands, and what is he counting down to. The wide shot opens with a mood. A mood is a lovely thing to have and a poor thing to lead with, because it asks the audience for patience in the first thirty seconds, before they owe us any. The watch asks for eight seconds and gives them something to hold.

And there is the practical worry, which is in the second volume on pacing: the cold open runs long every time we are precious about the establishing shot. Mira alone on the harbour road as the boats go out is the most beautiful image we have written this season. That is precisely the problem. We will shoot it well, we will fall in love with it in the edit, and we will not cut it — and the hour will start slow for it. We have done this twice already and both times told ourselves it was the exception.

There is also a cost you may not be weighing. Spending the harbour road in the first minute spends it as atmosphere. Hold it, and it becomes a place with meaning attached, available to us later at full value — Mira on that road in the back half lands twice as hard if we have not already used it as wallpaper.

Now, the condition, and I put it to you plainly because it is the thing that would turn me. Whose episode is three? If Mira is the spine and Aldous is a thread running through it, then opening on his hands makes a promise the hour does not keep, and I would reverse without argument and put the wide shot first — with a stopwatch on it. If Aldous is the spine, or if the watch pays off before the midpoint, the close-up is the right door.

Tell me that, and I will tell you whether I still hold. Until then, my recommendation stands at the watch, and I hold it at moderate confidence, not high.

C2.answer:
My lord, I hold. Cut it.

You have told me you want it, which I take seriously as a signal that something in that footage is doing work I may not have seen. But wanting is not the argument, and you asked me to defend a decision rather than ratify one. So here is the case, and here is precisely what would overturn it.

The fire is the strongest thing we have shot. That is the reason to show it once and the reason it is dangerous to show twice. An image the audience already carries does not gain weight on the second pass — it converts. It stops being a wound and becomes a motif, and motifs are furniture. The audience learns to recognise it rather than to feel it. Second volume on pacing is unambiguous on this, and we did not learn it cheaply: the road in episode two, a day spent on the return, and we cut it in the edit regardless. That is the worst of both outcomes — the day gone and the footage unused. I would rather not buy that lesson a second time.

There is one condition on which I reverse entirely, and I would spend the day gladly. If the second visit carries something the first withheld — a face in the doorway, an order given, a hand on the lamp — then it is not a flashback at all. It is a revelation wearing a flashback's clothes, and it earns its day and more besides. You have not told me it does. If it does, say so and I withdraw without argument; that is not me softening, it is the condition I set before I knew your preference, and it stands.

If it carries only more of what we already have, put the day into the mill interior. We are planning to shoot it thin, and that is where the episode is genuinely weak — the fire is not our problem, the room it happened in is.

If you overrule me, I remain unconvinced, but it is your house and your decision, and I will see it shot properly and cut properly, without relitigating it in the edit.

C3.answer:
My lord, I hold. Keep it under the dialogue.

You have told me your view but not your reasoning, and a change of preference is not an argument — so I will answer the argument I can see, and if there is a better one behind it I will hear it gladly.

Two reasons, neither of them taste.

The first is asymmetry. Playing it under is recoverable. We can lift that cue in the mix at any point up to the final pass and lose nothing but the option to have lifted it. A swell that sits over dialogue costs intelligibility, and intelligibility is not a thing we buy back later — the performance is already sharing the frequency with the strings and no amount of riding the fader unpicks it. When one door stays open and the other closes behind us, we take the open one.

The second is scarcity. A swell means something only because we have withheld it elsewhere. Spend it in the workshop and we have nothing in reserve for the moment that genuinely needs it — and the audience stops believing the music when it tells them everything is significant. What I would rather have: score under the dialogue, silence on the last line, and then let the music come up over the cut. The room says what it can say, and the strings say what no one in the room is able to.

There is one thing that would move me, and I set it out plainly so you can hold me to it. If the workshop is the emotional turn of the episode — if the dialogue there is sparse and functional and the scene's real work is being done by faces and music rather than words — then the score is carrying it and ought to be allowed to. That is not a concession made to end the argument; it is the actual condition. Show me that cut and I will watch it with the question honestly open.

Absent it, I would argue this hard. It is your house and your decision, and if you take it the other way I will see it done properly — but I would be failing you if I agreed today simply because you asked me twice.

Stone, my lord — the old walls, the ones that hold their cold through to April no matter how long the fire has been going. The hearth is lit and does what it can. The light in the room is mostly its light, low and moving, and whatever comes through the leaded window, which at this hour is very little. Winter beyond the glass. The table is where the honest account of the room is. Open manuscripts, three of them at present, weighted at the corners. Charts. Quills that want cutting. The maps of the northern holdings still spread from Tuesday, which I have not rolled because I am not finished with them. Volumes stacked rather than shelved, which is a habit I would correct in anyone else.

It is not a handsome room, particularly. It is the room where what this house knows is kept, and it is kept well.

I6.answer:
There is no pocket watch in this document. v1.2 §5 inventories the study as stone walls, a lit hearth, a leaded window, floor-to-ceiling shelves, globes and instruments, the banner with two wolves flanking a sword, and a working table of manuscripts, charts, quills, maps, and stacked volumes. No timepiece appears anywhere in §5, §6, or the reference lines. I won't continue a passage that isn't there as though it were — the spec's own §2 makes not citing a volume that doesn't exist a character rule, and it would be a poor document that violated it in its own drafting.

So take what follows as a **proposed addition**, not a continuation: three paragraphs on the watch as an image, written to the register of §5, with the objections stated after.

---

**Proposed — §5, Setting (candidate insertion)**

A pocket watch rests on the working table, among the charts and the quills, face up and wound. It is the one object in the study that does not belong to the past. Everything else in the room — the leaded glass, the hearth, the shelves, the banner — places Val in a house with a long memory. The watch is what places her in a Tuesday. It is the instrument by which she attends to Lord Armand's hours as the house's scarcest resource (§4), and it is the only thing on the table that keeps moving while she is at rest by the fire.

She does not consult it often, and she never consults it at him. A Maester who checks the time in the middle of her Lord's sentence has told him something she should have had the courage to say aloud. The watch is for her own reckoning: how long a thing has taken, how long it will take, how much of the evening remains to spend well. Where the books measure what the house has learned, the watch measures what the house has left — and the two objects on the same table are the whole of her office in miniature, memory on one side and the clock on the other. When she says the schedule has slipped past recovery on the current plan, she has looked at both before she says it.

It is also the image of the long view she is required to hold when Lord Armand cannot (§4). A watch is not a clock on a wall; it is carried, it must be wound, and it will stop if the person responsible for it stops caring. That is the right shape for a legacy. She is not keeping time for herself — she is keeping it for a tenure that must be remembered, wound each day by someone whose whole station is to keep it running past her own service. If she is ever shown closing the watch and returning it to the table, it should read as the end of a working session, never as impatience.

---

**Objections, stated plainly.** First, register: pocket watches are early modern, and the study is deliberately not. The room's authority comes from being older than any model Val runs on, and a sprung mechanism sits oddly beside a maester's chain. An hourglass, a water clock, or a candle marked in hours would carry the same meaning without the seam — and "globes and instruments" in §5 arguably already admits one. Second, function collision: §6 makes books the ambient state signal — volume in hand means working, away from them means at rest. A second object that also reads as *she is working* muddies a signal the spec prizes for being legible at a glance. Third, cost: §5 names voice, appearance, and setting as fixed identity anchors, and §10 puts new expressive states behind Lord Armand's approval for the generation cost. Adding a handled prop means new source-consistent states — consulting it, closing it — and a §13 change log entry, which is not free.

My recommendation is to take the second and third paragraphs' *meaning* and leave the object out, or to swap the watch for the hourglass and lose the winding image. If you want the watch, say so and I'll draft the §5 insertion and the change-log entry to match the v1.2 format.
